title: TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient - Microsoft Research
gist: Microsoft Research, UC Berkeley and Microsoft Security's open-source TokenEconomizer plugin learns from past coding-agent sessions in a repository (micro-skills, tool pruning, failure-loop intervention) to cut token costs 18.4–30.9% across 277 SWE-Bench tasks and five agent-model combinations without modifying the agent or model, while task success stayed broadly stable.

insights.claim: In profiling Claude Code on 60 SWE-Bench tasks, after a repository had at least five completed tasks, 30% of the agent's tool calls repeated an action from an earlier task in the same repository, versus only 7% matching another repository's history.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Repository-specific memory is a large untapped efficiency lever for agentic coding spend; watch for memory/context-caching features from agent vendors.
insights.quote: 30% of tool calls repeated an action from an earlier task in that repository

insights.claim: Claude Code received 23 tool descriptions on every turn in Microsoft Research's profiling, but 16 of them were never called, meaning most per-turn tool context was paid-for overhead.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Tool/MCP bloat directly inflates inference bills; dynamic tool loading is a likely product differentiator for coding agents.
insights.quote: The agent received 23 tool descriptions on every turn, but 16 were never called.

insights.claim: Failed coding-agent tasks are disproportionately expensive: the 17% of SWE-Bench tasks that Claude Code failed accounted for 32% of total spending.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Detecting stuck agents early is a cost-control priority; failure loops are where agentic token spend leaks.
insights.quote: The 17% of tasks that failed accounted for 32% of the spending.

insights.claim: AI coding agents typically start each session from scratch in the same codebase, rediscovering facts, loading unused tools, and repeating unsuccessful approaches, because most cost-reduction efforts focus on individual tasks rather than learning across sessions.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Cross-session learning is an underexploited axis for reducing agent token costs and improving enterprise ROI on coding agents.

insights.claim: Three popular open-source cost-saving plugins for coding agents, each built around a fixed strategy, lowered costs in some repositories but not others, suggesting effective cost control must adapt to each repository.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: One-size-fits-all token-saving tools are unreliable; adaptive, experience-driven controllers are the more defensible approach.
insights.quote: effective cost control must adapt to the repository, rather than apply the same strategy everywhere
insights.locator: We also tested three popular open-source plugins

insights.claim: Lowering a model's reasoning effort saved similar or larger amounts of cost than TokenEconomizer on SWE-Bench but caused substantial performance degradation, whereas TokenEconomizer cut costs without performance loss.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Simply dialing down reasoning is a false economy for coding agents; experience-based context trimming preserves quality while cutting spend.
insights.quote: lowering the model’s reasoning effort saved similar or larger amounts but led to substantial performance degradation

insights.claim: TokenEconomizer, an open-source plugin from UC Berkeley, Microsoft Research, and Microsoft Security, reduces coding-agent token waste by learning from past session logs in a repository without modifying the agent or its underlying model.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Black-box add-on cost controllers can work across any vendor's coding agent, commoditizing efficiency features and pressuring per-token revenue.

insights.claim: TokenEconomizer uses three mechanisms: micro-skills (one-line repository-specific notes added to context only after several sessions confirm a pattern), tool pruning (removing tools history suggests won't be used while keeping core command and edit tools), and failure-loop intervention (a judge model detects a stuck agent and suggests a different approach).
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: A reusable blueprint for agent cost control: learned context notes, dynamic tool sets, and stuck-loop detection.

insights.claim: In the open-source TokenEconomizer plugin, if an agent remains stuck after a redirect note, the system alerts the developer rather than stopping the work itself, and it requires no API key of its own and keeps learned data on the developer's machine.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Local-only, keyless design lowers enterprise adoption friction and data-privacy concerns for agent add-ons.
insights.quote: requires no API key of its own, and keeps what it learns on the developer’s machine

insights.claim: Across 277 SWE-Bench tasks from six repositories and five agent-model combinations, TokenEconomizer lowered mean cost per task by 18.4–30.9%, with Pass@1 rising in four of the five combinations; reported savings include the cost of its own model calls.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: An ~20–30% cut in agentic coding costs with stable quality is material for enterprise AI budgets and for vendors' per-token economics.

insights.claim: TokenEconomizer's savings grow with accumulated experience: early tasks can cost more while it learns, but cumulative costs fell below the default in every repository by the sixth task, and combining all three mechanisms delivered the largest reduction.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Payback on experience-driven agent tooling is fast (about six tasks per repo), favoring teams that work repeatedly in the same codebases.
insights.quote: cumulative costs fell below the default in every repository by the sixth task

insights.claim: TokenEconomizer's savings carried over beyond bug fixing: costs were 16.0–21.2% lower on Web-Bench sequential web development and 6.4–19.6% lower on security auditing, where every task is in a new repository.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Efficiency gains generalize across agent workloads, though smaller where there is no repository history to learn from.

themes.theme: Outlook: agents that learn to spend

insights.claim: Microsoft Research positions experience-driven controllers as a path toward coding agents that learn not only how to solve tasks but also how to spend computation more effectively, without changing the underlying agent or model.
insights.speaker: Brenda Potts
insights.so_what: Compute-efficiency learning layered on agents could slow token-consumption growth per task, relevant to inference-demand forecasts.
insights.quote: coding agents that learn not only how to solve tasks, but also how to spend computation more effectively
